# Ridgeline plots {#sec-ridgeline-plots} ::: {.callout-tip appearance='simple' icon=false} ***This graph is largely complete and just needs final proof reading.*** ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ridgeline_plots_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a categorical variable** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (continuous) variable** ::: :::: ## Description If we want to plot density curves but retain the interpretability of the axes, consider comparing multiple distributions using the [`ggridges` package](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/). ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"} Install packages. ::: ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} install.packages("ggridges") library(ggridges) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"} Squeezit was General Mills' fruit drink in a squeezable plastic bottle shaped like a little character, and every flavor came in a different color. We'll simulate how many seconds it took kids to squeeze out 60 bottles of each of six flavors. Each flavor gets its own average (`avg_seconds`), and `rgamma()` draws each bottle's time from a gamma distribution with the same shape (2.5) for every flavor. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 360 bottles every time you run the code below. ::: ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1998) squeezit_drinks <- tibble( bottle_id = 1:360, flavor = rep(c("Tropical", "Blue raspberry", "Strawberry", "Green punch", "Orange", "Cherry"), each = 60)) |> mutate(flavor = factor(flavor, levels = c("Cherry", "Orange", "Green punch", "Strawberry", "Blue raspberry", "Tropical")), avg_seconds = c(Tropical = 40, `Blue raspberry` = 32, Strawberry = 26, `Green punch` = 22, Orange = 18, Cherry = 12)[as.character(flavor)], seconds_to_finish = pmax(1, round(rgamma(n(), shape = 2.5, scale = avg_seconds / 2.5)))) |> select(bottle_id, flavor, seconds_to_finish) glimpse(squeezit_drinks) #> Rows: 360 #> Columns: 3 #> $ bottle_id 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8… #> $ flavor Tropical, Tropical, Tr… #> $ seconds_to_finish 55, 18, 48, 11, 23, 94… ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution Ridgeline plots stack one density curve per group, which makes them good for comparing many groups at once. All six flavors here share the same *kind* of distribution: most bottles are empty fairly quickly, and a few take a long time. What changes from flavor to flavor is the scale. Below we'll move from the bottles, to a picture, to the formula. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first five tropical bottles. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} head(squeezit_drinks, 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: These five bottles took anywhere from 11 to 55 seconds. The summary below shows that the mean is above the median for every flavor (a sign of right skew), and that the standard deviation grows with the mean. The ratio of the two (`cv`) stays between about 0.5 and 0.7 for every flavor. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} squeezit_drinks |> group_by(flavor) |> summarise(mean = mean(seconds_to_finish), median = median(seconds_to_finish), sd = sd(seconds_to_finish), cv = sd / mean) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: The ridgeline plot below adds a line at each flavor's median (`quantile_lines = TRUE` with `quantiles = 2`). Every ridge has a hump on the left and a tail on the right. Moving up from cherry to tropical, the humps slide right and the tails get longer, but the overall shape stays the same (the extra bumps, like the one in the tropical ridge, are noise from having only 60 bottles per flavor). ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} ggplot(squeezit_drinks, aes(x = seconds_to_finish, y = flavor, fill = flavor)) + ggridges::geom_density_ridges(alpha = 2/3, quantile_lines = TRUE, quantiles = 2, color = "#F5F5F5", show.legend = FALSE) + labs(x = "Seconds to finish", y = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ridgeline_plots_files/figure-html/draw_ridges-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: Each flavor's runs come from a [gamma distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_distribution) with a shared shape ($k$) and its own scale ($\theta$): $$ X_{\text{flavor}} \sim \text{Gamma}(k = 2.5, \; \theta_{\text{flavor}}), \quad \theta = \frac{\text{avg seconds}}{2.5} $$ The mean of a gamma distribution is $k\theta$ and its standard deviation is $\sqrt{k}\,\theta$, so their ratio is $1 / \sqrt{k} = 1 / \sqrt{2.5} \approx 0.63$ no matter the flavor. That's why the `cv` column stays near 0.63 and why the ridges all have the same shape: changing $\theta$ stretches a ridge along the `x` axis without changing its shape. This is the same distribution we used for the Talkboy messages in @sec-freq-poly. Try giving one flavor a larger `shape` in `rgamma()` and its ridge becomes more symmetric. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Create labels with `labs()` - Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data` - Map `seconds_to_finish` to the `x` axis - Map `flavor` to the `y` axis and `fill` - Add the `ggridges::geom_density_ridges()` layer (with `alpha` set to `2/3`) - Remove the legend with `show.legend = FALSE` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_ridges <- labs( title = "Squeezit", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Seconds to squeeze out a whole bottle", x = "Seconds to finish", y = "Flavor", fill = "Flavor") ggp2_ridges <- ggplot(data = squeezit_drinks, aes(x = seconds_to_finish, y = flavor, fill = flavor)) + ggridges::geom_density_ridges(alpha = 2/3, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_ridges + labs_ridges ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: Ridgeline plots are excellent for comparing continuous distributions across groups. ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ridgeline_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_ridges-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: :::
